items.title: Morning update
items.content:
Morning update
Good morning Middle East Eye readers,
Here are the latest developments:
An Israeli attack on an apartment in Gaza City has killed a senior Palestinian security official alongside his wife and two daughters, aged 13 and 15. According to the interior ministry, the man was identified as the director of the Internal Security Service in northern Gaza, Muhammad Majid Abu al-Awf, 47. This marks the second killing of a security official in Gaza in less than 24 hours, with the previous attack killing director-general of the Internal Security Service, Naim Mohammed Abu Nahl.
Iran's First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref said that Tehran is not concerned about the US naval blockade, the semi-official Tasnim news agency reported. He indicated the country's self-reliance with the increase of cargo clearance through its non-southern borders and added that reserves of strategic goods remain strong.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said that two "offending" oil tankers on the southern and eastern coasts of the Strait of Hormuz suffered explosions. "These tankers, believing they were secretly trying to pass through the fake Strait of Hormuz route, were prevented from passing by naval mines, causing a massive explosion and fire," it said in a statement.
The Saudi-led coalition's spokesperson said in a post on X that it targeted "operational capabilities" at Yemen's Hodeidah port. Additionally, Turki al-Maliki added that a number of targets in northern Yemen's Saada and Amran governorates were destroyed.
The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted and destroyed four drones in Ras Tanura, located in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province. The coalition's spokesperson Turki al-Maliki indicated that a number of fragments had fallen as a result of the interception, with no casualties reported in the initial assessment.
A US poll shows Trump's approval at 37 percent, with strong disapproval over his handling of the Iran war.

items.title: More on Israeli strike targeting apartment in Gaza City
items.content:
More on Israeli strike targeting apartment in Gaza City
An Israeli attack on an apartment in Gaza City has killed a senior Palestinian security official alongside his wife and two daughters, aged 13 and 15.
According to the Interior Ministry, the man was identified as the director of the Internal Security Service in northern Gaza, Muhammad Majid Abu al-Awf, 47.
The ministry slammed the attack as a "horrific massacre" and called for "urgent and genuine action to restrain the occupation from committing further crimes against innocent civilians" in the Gaza Strip.
"The Ministry of Interior and National Security condemns this heinous crime against security personnel and affirms that it comes within the context of ongoing attempts to undermine the security apparatus in the Gaza Strip in an effort to spread chaos within Palestinian society."
Earlier, the director-general of the Internal Security Service, Naim Mohammed Abu Nahl, was assassinated in an Israeli strike west of Gaza City.

items.title: Yemen's Houthis say they attacked Saudi oil refinery and Riyadh financial district
items.content:
Nov 25 (Reuters) - Yemen's Houthis said on Wednesday they had attacked Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery and Riyadh's financial district.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the refinery attack caused fires and that the group had attacked the financial district in three phases.
The Saudi-led coalition said earlier on Wednesday that air defences had intercepted and destroyed four drones in Ras Tanura in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province.

items.title: ‘Nature’s Ozempic’: oat sales soar as shoppers seek out foods that mimic effect of GLP-1s
items.content:
Porridge emerges as trend’s poster child with consumers looking to foods that help them feel full for longer, says Waitrose
Sales of filling foods such as porridge oats that mimic the effect of taking weight-loss medication are booming on the back of social media hype billing them as “nature’s Ozempic” or “oatzempic”.
Sales of Waitrose Scottish Oats are up 124% this year, according to the retailer’s annual food and drink report, which dissects the biggest trends sweeping the grocery aisles. A poll conducted for the report revealed that 64% of shoppers are “actively choosing to eat foods like oats that keep us feeling fuller for longer”.

items.title: Saudi foreign minister calls Bahrain, Egypt counterparts to discuss conflict with Houthis
items.content:
Saudi foreign minister calls Bahrain, Egypt counterparts to discuss conflict with Houthis
Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud has held separate phone calls with his Bahraini and Egyptian counterparts to discuss the latest regional developments and the ongoing conflict with Yemen's Houthis.
In a statement on X, the Saudi Foreign Ministry said that Bahrain's Abdullatif bin Rashid Al Zayani and Egypt's Badr Abdelatty condemned the ongoing Houthi attacks on Yemen and the kingdom.
It added that they also discussed "ongoing efforts to reduce tensions and enhance security and stability" in the region.

items.title: China-linked battery projects could receive UK funding despite security warnings
items.content:
China-made lithium-ion batteries, which are relatively low-cost, dominate Ofgem project shortlist
A string of battery projects linked to China are expected to be granted UK state subsidies despite deepening fears over the risk of foreign interference they could pose to Europe’s energy systems.
Ofgem, Great Britain’s energy regulator, published a provisional shortlist for a new “long duration” energy storage scheme in June. The list was dominated by projects relying on lithium-ion batteries, which are typically manufactured in China and operated with Chinese software.

items.title: In charts: how power could shift in Europe’s big year of elections
items.content:
More than half of EU voters will go to the polls in the next 12 months, with the far right targeting significant gains. We set out the political landscape and trends
Europe is entering a ‘supercycle’ of national elections. Their outcomes could shake the EU’s foundations
Over the coming 12 months, more than half of the EU’s electorate will go to the polls in elections that could change the direction of the continent, with attention focused on voters in four of the bloc’s five biggest states.

items.title: IRGC Navy says two 'violating' oil tankers hit naval mine in Hormuz Strait
items.content:
IRGC Navy says two 'violating' oil tankers hit naval mine in Hormuz Strait
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said that two "offending" oil tankers on the southern and eastern coasts of the Strait of Hormuz suffered explosions.
"These tankers, believing they were secretly trying to pass through the fake Strait of Hormuz route, were prevented from passing by naval mines, causing a massive explosion and fire," it said in a statement.
"We warn all crews of ships with navigation and positioning systems turned off, be careful not to let the lies of American officials lead you to the explosion and fire of naval mines," the IRGC added.

items.title: The Russian army’s secret death toll – podcast
items.content:
Vladimir Putin has always kept the number of soldiers killed in Ukraine a secret, but at one point 720 were dying in 24 hours. Pjotr Sauer reports. Send your comments and questions to
tif.questions@theguardian.com
Russia has kept the death toll of its soldiers in the Ukraine war a carefully guarded secret. Now documents leaked to the Guardian have
revealed its true scale
. The Guardian’s Russia affairs correspondent,
Pjotr Sauer
, tells
Helen Pidd
what reporters have discovered.
Two groups of hackers accessed Russia’s main statistics database last month and discovered a cache of 11m death certificates that revealed nearly 500,000 Russian losses in Ukraine since 2022. Among these were 1,000 – the equivalent of a whole regiment – who took their own lives.

items.title: Watch: Gaza declares meningitis alert as health ministry blames Israeli restrictions
items.content:
Watch: Gaza declares meningitis alert as health ministry blames Israeli restrictions
Gaza’s health ministry has issued an "epidemiological alert" across the territory, warning that a "shocking" increase in meningitis infections puts hundreds of thousands of lives at risk, particularly children.
The ministry urged the World Health Organization and Unicef to launch an emergency response.
Dr Nidal Ghunaim, deputy director general of primary healthcare for public health, reported 272 cases in October. He described the figure as more than eight times the usual monthly average of 30 to 50.
Meningitis has killed 15 people this year, Ghunaim said, including five during the surge from August to October.
The ministry described the outbreak as an "inevitable result of the destruction of infrastructure, overcrowding of shelters, mixing of drinking water with sewage, and the disaster being exacerbated by flooding due to rain".
Gaza’s health ministry has issued an epidemiological alert over a “shocking” surge in meningitis infections, warning that hundreds of thousands of lives are at risk, particularly children. The ministry has called for an emergency response. https://t.co/imC1ibBbYr

items.title: Is the war in the Middle East spilling into Europe?
items.content:
Is the war in the Middle East spilling into Europe?
From cyberattacks on fridges to threats against military bases hosting US forces, European authorities have accused Iran of planning attacks on their countries.
Iran has rejected those accusations.
Meanwhile, the war between Iran, the US and Israel has been in stalemate for months. And Iranian officials have threatened to bomb American bases in Europe should the US attack the country.
So, what’s happening? Middle East Eye's Maya Saad takes a look.

items.content:
Failure to implement previous reports means institutional racism, misogyny and homophobia still present in force
Metropolitan police still institutionally racist and misogynist, says report
From the Stephen Lawrence inquiry in 1999 to Louise Casey’s landmark review in 2023, successive reports on the Metropolitan police have arrived at the same damning conclusion: Britain’s largest police force is institutionally racist.
It will, therefore, come as little surprise that three years after Casey’s report, an independent review led by Gillian Fairfield has found that institutional racism, misogyny and homophobia persist within the force.

The Metropolitan police remain institutionally racist, misogynistic and homophobic three years after a damning review into the force’s culture, a report has found.
The investigation by Gillian Fairfield found “fundamental, systemic issues” and “institutional defensiveness” still existed in Britain’s biggest police force, which has struggled “to acknowledge racism as a structural problem”.

items.title: England has largest frailty gap out of 31 countries, study finds
items.content:
People from lowest socioeconomic group in all countries studied had higher frailty scores than those in highest socioeconomic group
England has the largest gap between higher and lower socioeconomic groups when it comes to frailty compared with 30 other countries, a major study has found.
The research, led by academics at King’s College London and published in BMC Medicine, looked at levels of frailty in 71,703 people from 31 countries including England, the US, China, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Sweden, Greece, Cyprus, Latvia and Lithuania.

items.title: 11 جريحا في هجوم بمسيّرة على برج في الرياض والتحالف بقيادة السعودية يتوعد بالرد "بحزم"
items.content:
11 جريحا في هجوم بمسيّرة على برج في الرياض والتحالف بقيادة السعودية يتوعد بالرد "بحزم"
أصيب 11 شخصا الثلاثاء في هجوم بمسيّرة استهدف أحد أبراج مركز الملك عبدالله المالي في الرياض، بينهم اثنان على الأقل بحالة حرجة، فيما تود التحالف بقيادة السعودية بالرد "بحزم". وفي اليمن، أصدر التحالف تحذيرا لإخلاء ميناء الحديدة، بينما هدّد الحوثيون باستهداف ميناء جدة والموانئ السعودية على البحر الأحمر في حال قصف الحديدة. وفي مضيق هرمز، أفادت طهران بتضرر سفينة حاويات جراء اصطدامها بلغم بحري، وسط استمرار التوترات في حركة الملاحة.

items.title: Kushner says Israel is becoming a 'pariah' as his Board of Peace plans stall
items.content:
Kushner says Israel is becoming a 'pariah' as his Board of Peace plans stall
Israel
is on track to become a “global pariah” over its genocide in the Gaza Strip, Jared Kushner,
US
President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and diplomatic envoy, said in an interview released on Monday.
“Israel could rise from the tragedy of October 7, [and] be much more secure and much more integrated into the world, or they can go on the current trajectory, which is to trend toward global-pariah status,” Kushner said in an interview with New York Magazine.
The remarks are notable given Kushner’s longtime advocacy for Israel and efforts to put it at the centre of a new regional security architecture in the Middle East.
Kushner is a longtime family friend of
Israeli
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and created the controversial Board of Peace which was supposed to oversee Gaza’s reconstruction.
Read more:
Kushner says Israel is becoming a 'pariah' as his Board of Peace plans stall
US special envoy Jared Kushner pictured last week (Hannah McKay/AFP)

JERUSALEM, Nov 24 (Reuters) - Israel'sYashar party, led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, said on Tuesday it agreed to sign a coalition pact with a right-wing opposition party as it seeks to form a government following last month's election.
Yashar said that Eisenkot had met with Avigdor Lieberman, head of the Israel Our Home party, earlier on Tuesday and they agreed on a deal afterward, the first such alliance since the election.

items.title: China's Huawei convicted in sprawling US criminal trial over Iran business
items.content:
By Karen Freifeld
NEW YORK, Nov 25 (Reuters) - Chinese telecoms equipment maker Huawei was convicted by a jury in New York City on Tuesday in a sprawling US criminal case on charges that it deceived banks about its business in Iran andconspired to steal trade secrets from American companies.
The verdict came in a criminal case that began in 2018, with the US government the following year placing Huawei on a trade blacklist that restricted its access to US technology amid American concerns that Huawei posed national security risks.

items.title: Yemeni government forces report nearly 700 strikes against Houthis
items.content:
Yemeni government forces report nearly 700 strikes against Houthis
Yemeni government forces say they carried out 697 strikes targeting the Iran-aligned Houthis over the past few hours, the army’s spokesperson Majed al-Nuzaili said.
Al-Nuzaili said in a post on X that the attacks included 17 air strikes, 32 drone attacks, 28 rocket attacks and 620 artillery attacks targeting Houthi positions, gatherings, vehicles and weapons depots.
These strikes killed 97 Houthi commanders and fighters and destroyed or damaged 76 vehicles and combat assets, he said.
The government forces and their allies continue to repel Houthi attacks in Taiz amid ongoing clashes on the Marib and al Jawf fronts, he added.

items.title: Who wins from Baghdad's move to clip Kurdish autonomy - the US or Iran?
items.content:
Who wins from Baghdad's move to clip Kurdish autonomy - the US or Iran?
Submitted by
Sean Mathews
on
Tue, 11/24/2026 - 21:41
Iraq's federal government said it was moving to seize control of border posts and energy facilities controlled by the KRG
Iranian trucks waiting to cross back into Iran in the Penjwen district in Iraq's semi-autonomous Kurdistan Region in September 2026 (Safin Hamid/AFP)
Off
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has said Baghdad will take over all of Kurdistan's border crossings and several oil fields that the autonomous region controls, in a move that was widely condemned by the region’s leaders as a step to clip their autonomy.
Baghdad’s decision comes at a time of internal division in the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) and as the Middle East braces for a potential new US-Israeli attack on Iran.
Under American pressure, Zaidi recently attempted to crack down on Kataib Hezbollah, a powerful Shia militia in Iraq aligned with Iran, which officials in Baghdad say has earned hundreds of millions of dollars from smuggling oil.
Zaidi's spokesperson Sabah al-Numan said on Tuesday that, based on those findings, Baghad would take control of "all border crossings in the Kurdistan Region".
He added that Zaidi directed the oil ministry "to manage all oil fields" that are under Kurdish "security authority" despite lying outside the Kurdistan Region, in the provinces of Diyala, Kirkuk, Salaheddine and Nineveh. Zaidi also ordered the Kurdistan government not to approve oil exports except through the federal oil ministry.
The KRG is guaranteed some autonomy under Iraq’s 2005 constitution, but its control of border crossings has been a longstanding issue of dispute, as have energy resources.
Does Iran or the US benefit?
The move by Baghdad’s central government to wrest control of the posts alongside energy facilities comes as it tries to seal new energy deals with Turkey and looks to pipelines through the region to bypass the Strait of Hormuz.
The KRG region has been a close US security partner for decades, but the last US troops left Erbil, the region's capital, in September, completing a full US withdrawal from Iraq. The region faced hundreds of Iranian missile and drone strikes
during this year's war
.
Inside the Iraqi Kurdish city caught between the US and Iran
Read More »
Experts debated whether Baghdad's decision was made with the agreement of Iran, which has called on the KRG to rein in Kurdish opposition groups, or the US which has lobbied regional states to consolidate federal power.
Tom Barrack, the US ambassador to Turkey and Middle East envoy, has been the main proponent of this view.
Yesar Al-Maleki, a Gulf analyst at the Middle East Economic Survey, said Zaidi was taking advantage of a shift in the US.
“Washington, has clearly shifted its Iraq policy toward greater centralisation; the PUK and KDP are no longer presenting a united front in Iraqi politics; and the US military withdrawal has given Baghdad greater security bandwidth,” he wrote on X.
'Tehran fears an uprising'
But Fabrice Balanche, a Kurdish expert,
said
Baghdad’s move would benefit Iran as well, given its suspicion of the US and Israel using the region as a base to attack it.
“Iraq’s determination to dismantle the KRG by depriving it of its economic resources must be seen in the context of the conflict between the US and Iran,” he wrote in an essay.
“Tehran fears that Iraqi Kurdistan could serve as a rear base for an uprising in Iranian Kurdistan,” he added.
The KRG is at its weakest in years. The region is dominated by two family dynasties, the Barzani family in Erbil, which leads the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), and the Talabani family in Sulaymaniyah, which leads the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK).
The PUK withdrew from the region's parliament in November and its leader, Bafel Talabani, said the region was already living "the reality of two governments and two administrations".
Kurdistan Region Prime Minister Masrour Barzani said his government was "surprised" by Zaidi's decisions, calling them "completely unacceptable".
But both parties put aside their differences to issue a relatively mild censure of Baghdad’s decision.
“The Kurdistan Region has never sought anything beyond the rights guaranteed to it under the Iraqi Constitution. However, its constitutional rights have been violated over the years,” the statement said.
“We stress that all parties must abide by the Constitution and that, should any dispute arise between the Kurdistan Region and the Federal Government, the Constitution must serve as the ultimate point of reference,” the statement added.

items.title: Climate scientists urge US lawmakers to vote no on sweeping permitting bill
items.content:
Open letter warns Baaja, intended to expedite energy and infrastructure projects, will cause irreversible climate harm
A group of more than 120 climate scientists have urged US lawmakers to not pass contentious legislation to speed up the building of energy projects, datacenters and other infrastructure, amid a growing backlash to the sweeping permitting bill.
In
an open letter to members of the House of Representatives
, the collection of Earth and social sciences researchers expressed “deep concern” that the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (or Baaja) weakens environmental laws, locks in new fossil fuel projects without recourse and delivers only minor cuts to planet-heating emissions.

items.title: 'Unlawful de facto exemption': US sitting on 12-year backlog of alleged Israeli rights violations
items.content:
'Unlawful de facto exemption': US sitting on 12-year backlog of alleged Israeli rights violations
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Tue, 11/24/2026 - 18:17
A report from the Office of The Inspector General has raised concerns that the US has given Israel an 'exemption' from the Leahy Law
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio pictured last month (Oliver Contreras/AFP)
Off
The US Department of State has a 12-year backlog of alleged cases of gross human rights violations in Israel to adjudicate, because the agency has made little effort to trace the end point of US military assistance there, a
report
quietly posted online by the Office of the Inspector General (OIG) last month showed.
The findings "demonstrate that the Department has created an unlawful de facto exemption to the law for Israel", Charles Blaha, a state department official who retired in 2023, wrote in a piece for
Just Security
on Monday.
The OIG report hones in on the application of the Leahy Law, which prohibits US assistance to any foreign security forces unit if the secretary of state has credible information that such a unit has committed "gross violations of human rights".
In a
September 2025 report
to Congress, the state department said the only units it had assessed to be ineligible for US security assistance were in Ukraine, Egypt and Jordan - even though Israel had previously been cited as having non-traceable assistance (NTA).
The NTA means the state department "cannot identify recipient units in advance of the transfer of assistance or training, or the units are not known with sufficient detail to make Leahy vetting possible", the OIG report said.
It concluded that the state department "had not developed or distributed comprehensive guidance and training to help staff implement NTA vetting requirements", and that nearly half of all missions overseas "did not respond to annual requirements to certify if a country was receiving NTA".
"For those countries receiving NTA, additional certifications are necessary to validate that foreign security forces are complying with US requirements," the report added.
In April 2024, under the Biden administration, the state department determined that five Israeli security units had committed grave human rights violations.
But
it then said
that four of them had remedied the violations, and could still receive US security assistance, while the fifth unit would "remain indefinitely eligible while the State Department engaged with the government of Israel 'on identifying a path to effective remediation of this unit'".
But the state department "has never delivered a list of ineligible Israeli units to the government of Israel. Not once", Blaha
wrote
in June of that year.
War on Gaza
Blaha, who was the director of two different offices in the Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights, and Labor in the state department from 2013 to 2023, said on Monday that his former employer "never officially explained its failure to enforce Leahy with regard to Israel, except to say that investigations are ongoing or cases are being reviewed".
"Behind the scenes, opponents of applying the law to Israel at the State Department and on the National Security Council have advanced specious, legally irrelevant policy arguments," he wrote.
Israel likely to lose Gaza genocide case if ICJ follows Myanmar ruling, Tel Aviv scholar says
Read More »
"During the Biden administration, Secretary of State Antony Blinken reportedly refused to implement Leahy with regard to Israel due to speculation that it would jeopardize unrelated ceasefire negotiations. The argument was far-fetched in 2024, and is obsolete now that Israel has signed the October 2025 Gaza peace plan."
The US has always had tools at its disposal to pressure allies to change direction, and especially ones who are dependent on US military assistance.
These tools include the
Leahy Law
, which prohibits US military assistance to units that violate human rights laws; the
Export Control Act
, which bars the transfer of weapons abroad if they could end up threatening US national security; and section 620I of the
Foreign Assistance Act
, which stipulates that the US government cannot provide weapons to a government that is hindering access to humanitarian aid.
The Export Control Act, in particular, states that countries can only receive US weapons if they use them defensively, not offensively.
Former state department official Hala Rharrit previously
told Middle East Eye
that its precisely why Blinken deferred to the refrain that “Israel has a right to defend itself”.
“It's not by accident [that] the words that [came] out of his mouth,” she said.
Loopholes
In December 2024, a month before the Biden administration left power,
five Palestinians living in the US and Gaza
filed a lawsuit
against Blinken over accusations that Washington was not abiding by the Leahy Law and therefore allowing Israel to carry out its unprecedented assault on Gaza.
That assault has since been assessed to be a genocide by both the United Nations and Holocaust scholars. More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since 7 October 2023, with at least 10,000 more missing under the rubble, the Lancet medical journal
previously estimated
.
The lawsuit, which was filed with the help of the rights group Democracy for the Arab World Now (Dawn), outlined how the Biden administration created loopholes that allowed Israel to continue committing human rights violations without a suspension of aid from Washington.
One such loophole was the state department's establishment of the "Israel Leahy Vetting Forum", which the lawsuit said was designed "to impede any prompt and effective determination that Israeli units have committed" gross violations of human rights.
Dawn was founded by the late MEE columnist Jamal Khashoggi. One of the plaintiffs in the lawsuit is Gaza-born Ahmed Moor, who is
running for the US Senate
in 2028.
Blaha, who is now a senior adviser to Dawn,
said in 2024
that "the standard for ineligibility is almost impossibly high" when it comes to Israel.
"A determination that any Israeli unit is Leahy-ineligible rests with the deputy secretary of state. This is true for no other country in the world," he said. "Such determinations are routinely made at the working level, by experts versed in the Leahy Law and knowledgeable about the foreign security units in question."
The underlying culprit, he added, "is lack of political will".

items.title: US judge permanently bars Trump from punishing rights groups who liaise with ICC
items.content:
US judge permanently bars Trump from punishing rights groups who liaise with ICC
A US federal judge on Monday
permanently barred
the Trump administration from punishing rights groups who liaise with the International Criminal Court (ICC).
The ruling extends to all Americans, and not just the plaintiffs in the case.
Judge Jesse Furman of the Southern District of New York first issued a
temporary injunction
last month.
This week he ruled that while "the Government effectively requests that the Court reconsider its earlier decisions ... there is no merit to that request".
"Put simply, Plaintiffs demonstrate that the Services Prohibition is a content-based restriction on speech and that it is not narrowly tailored to serve compelling state interests," Furman wrote.

items.content:
Abelardo de la Espriella to take control of operation trying to free at least 20 hostages
Colombia’s president has arrived at the scene of an hours-long standoff between security services and gunmen holding at least 20 people hostage inside a supermarket in Cartagena, a popular tourist city.
Abelardo de la Espriella’s motorcade arrived in Cartagena on Tuesday night, Agence France-Presse reported, where he will ostensibly take control of an operation involving scores of officers, the navy and special forces.

items.title: Kushner says Israel is becoming a 'pariah' as his Board of Peace plans stall
items.content:
Kushner says Israel is becoming a 'pariah' as his Board of Peace plans stall
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Tue, 11/24/2026 - 18:33
US president's son-in-law has faced funding issues and delays in his attempt to reconstruct Gaza with Gulf cash
US special envoy Jared Kushner pictured last week (Hannah McKay/AFP)
Off
Israel
is on track to become a “global pariah” over its genocide in the Gaza Strip, Jared Kushner,
US
President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and diplomatic envoy, said in an interview released on Monday.
“Israel could rise from the tragedy of October 7, [and] be much more secure and much more integrated into the world, or they can go on the current trajectory, which is to trend toward global-pariah status,” Kushner said in an interview with New York Magazine.
The remarks are notable given Kushner’s longtime advocacy for Israel and efforts to put it at the centre of a new regional security architecture in the Middle East.
Kushner is a longtime family friend of
Israeli
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and created the controversial Board of Peace which was supposed to oversee Gaza’s reconstruction.
It is not clear what motivated Kushner’s comments, but his bid to be a Middle East peacemaker and builder has not held up, with Israel attacking the besieged enclave and much hyped-up reconstruction projects stalled.
The enclave was pummelled by Israel in a genocide of Palestinians after the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attack on southern Israel.
More than 70,000 Palestinians were killed in the onslaught with 1,679 people killed in Israeli strikes since the October 2025 “ceasefire” Kushner helped broker was announced.
The UN estimates it will cost $70bn to rebuild Gaza, but Kushner has struggled to launch even a small $2.45bn rebuilding project involving 66 projects across the enclave. Kushner blamed "different delays on different things, for whatever reason", during a presentation on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York City in September.
Israel kills UN worker and two others across Gaza as attacks on Palestinians continue
Read More »
Kushner essentially envisioned the Board of Peace running the Gaza Strip with a combination of Gulf financing, supranational advisers, some Palestinian technocrats and an outside security force.
But the Gulf states have withheld funding and now face economic contractions because of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Middle East Eye
revealed
in May that Aryeh Lightstone, one of the key US officials overseeing the US’s post-war planning for Gaza, went to Saudi Arabia in the spring to lobby for funding but returned empty handed.
The much discussed international stabilisation force has not entered the territory and the Palestinian technocrats supposed to run day-to-day affairs also remain in Cairo.
The Times of Israel reported that “less than 2 percent” of the $17bn in pledges the Board of Peace was given have been met. In a sign of the board’s desperation, senior envoy Nickolay Mladenov travelled to Moscow on Monday and said Russia could contribute as a permanent member of the UN Security Council.

items.title: Britain must stand firm against Nusseibeh's UN candidacy
items.content:
Britain must stand firm against Nusseibeh's UN candidacy
Submitted by
David Hearst
on
Tue, 11/24/2026 - 18:13
Appointing her as secretary general would effectively put the UAE and Israel, two nations determined to fuel regional chaos, in charge of the United Nations
Emirati diplomat Lana Nusseibeh addresses the United Nations General Assembly in New York on 27 September 2025 (Charly Triballeau/AFP)
Off
For as long as anyone can remember,
US
President Donald Trump and
Israeli
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have used every platform to attack the United Nations, and every opportunity to defund its life-saving institutions.
Netanyahu called the UN a “
swamp of antisemitism
” that had to be drained.
Trump called the UN
Human Rights Council
“craven hypocrites” who had little to say about the persecution of Christians, and accused Unesco - with its “ceaseless promotion of mass migration” - of actively destroying the greatest culture in history (ie the US).
Long before Israel claimed, without proof, that the UN Relief and Works Agency (Unrwa) was
infiltrated by Hamas
, Trump
withdrew funding
from Unrwa, cutting off the only UN agency dedicated specifically to
Palestinian
refugees.
How curious, then, that so much effort is being put into placing their candidate as the next secretary general of the UN.
Their candidate is
Lana Nusseibeh
, a
British-educated
diplomat from an old Palestinian family, who served as the
UAE
’s permanent representative to the UN from 2013 to 2024.
During those years, the country she represented actively worked against everything the UN was trying to do to stabilise the Middle East and Africa.
The Emirati network
The UAE funded a military coup in
Egypt
. In
Libya
, it ran guns, armoured vehicles and surveillance equipment in a constant airlift to the
renegade general Khalifa Haftar
in Benghazi and Tobruk, despite a
UN arms embargo
.
Between April and July 2025, more than 30 military Il-76 flights were
recorded
between the UAE and Benghazi, some of which were operated by private firms contracted by Abu Dhabi.
Alongside the Egyptian military, the UAE
plotted the downfall
of parliamentary democracy in
Tunisia
. In
Sudan
, it has provided
arms shipments
, intelligence and logistics to the
Rapid Support Forces
(RSF). It established two airfields - Berbera in breakaway Somaliland, and
Bosaso in Puntland
- to act as logistics hubs.
The UAE is attempting to leverage conflict and separatism in Libya, Sudan and the Horn of Africa, to project its power and economic influence without a territorial footprint. It acts mainly through proxies.
The objective is to position Abu Dhabi as a key security player and economic partner at strategic ports and global trade chokepoints, without the appearance of a traditional military footprint
During this campaign, the UN has been at the forefront of bringing the atrocities committed by UAE proxies to light. UN agencies have published a
series of reports
on ethnic cleansing by the RSF, the UAE’s primary actor in Sudan, which Abu Dhabi arms and bankrolls.
Last year, the UN Human Rights Office published details of widespread killings, rape, torture and abductions committed during a three-day RSF offensive on the Zamzam displacement camp, which killed
more than 1,000 civilians
.
This past February, the
Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan
found all the hallmarks of genocide in the RSF’s
500-day siege
and sacking of El Fasher, the capital of North Darfur.
The sum effect of the UAE’s campaign in the Middle East and Africa can be measured in the latest World Food Programme (WFP)
report
on global famine. The UAE and Israel are fighting and fomenting strife in three of the five countries whose populations are identified by the WFP as facing catastrophe and risk of famine - Gaza, Nigeria, South Sudan,
Yemen
and Sudan. The conflicts it backs are the key drivers of famine, displacement and refugees.
The WFP, one of the main providers of food in Gaza, recently had to cut aid
by a third
, because it received half as much funding this year for its operations in Palestine.
Denying the undeniable
Put another way, the UAE exports more than just oil and gas. In Sudan alone, its exports amount to
19.5 million people
facing acute hunger, and millions of others either internally displaced or fleeing to Chad, South Sudan, Egypt, Ethiopia or the Central African Republic.
The UAE’s covert interventions are highly structured, never ad hoc. And they are interlinked: supply routes through
Chad and Libya
have been used to arm the RSF in Sudan since April 2023, UN experts found, while the UAE has also
shipped in mercenaries
from Colombia.
The objective is to position Abu Dhabi as a key security player and economic partner at strategic ports and global trade chokepoints, without the appearance of a traditional military footprint.
Who is Lana Nusseibeh, the UAE diplomat in the race to become next UN secretary-general?
Read More »
Almost everything it does is deniable - and it was Nusseibeh’s role for 11 years at the UN to keep it that way. Her second task was to
forge ties with Israel
, turning the Emiratis into Israel’s strongest diplomatic and military ally in the Arab world - far more important than the two Arab states with negotiated peace deals,
Jordan
and Egypt.
Netanyahu is a natural partner for UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed. Both think political Islam is an existential enemy. Mohammed bin Zayed is obsessed by the reach of the
Muslim Brotherhood
, believing it has power far beyond Egypt, its country of origin.
If Mohammed bin Zayed’s cohort of dictators saw the
Arab Spring
in Tunisia, Egypt and Yemen as a personal threat, the Emirati ruler saw it also as an ideological one.
In his jihad against political Islam, Mohammed bin Zayed sees the Brotherhood everywhere, ascribing to it a presence and a role far greater than it actually possesses. He sees the Brotherhood in London, Paris and Berlin - and the Emiratis are hard at work funding and tutoring the racist European far right in
Islamophobia
.
Reshaping the region
Outside Mohammed bin Zayed’s jihad, the truth about the Muslim Brotherhood is ironically quite different.
While the movement is organisationally at its weakest, after decades of oppression and imprisonment in Egypt, Jordan and Tunisia,
Israel’s genocide in Gaza
helped political Islam recover to an extent not thought possible just a few years ago.
The Gaza
genocide
has lowered the barriers between political Islam and the secular left - barriers once so high that they fatally weakened the first wave of democratic revolution in Egypt and Tunisia for more than a decade.
The key distinction in the diaspora now is less whether you are secular or Islamist, but whether you are active or passive in organising against genocide.
Can anyone imagine what Israel would do to the UN, and to all those fact-finding reports and investigations bubbling away inside, with its own candidate running the institution?
Both the UAE and Israel have big ambitions to “reshape” the Middle East, away from the dominance of traditional nation states. Both are small countries, dwarfed in population and land by larger neighbours, and their aim is to dominate as technological and military hubs by splitting up the others.
Israel says this openly about
Syria
, and allows academics to speculate about dismembering Egypt. The UAE is only too happy to encourage these plans, because its principal target is its lumbering neighbour,
Saudi Arabia
.
Both Israel and the UAE are avid users of mobile phone software to spy on and
target dissidents
abroad.
Pro-Israel lobbying groups are too quick to recognise the importance of Nusseibeh’s work and reward her for it. In a
revealing
column, Jake Wallis Simons, former editor of the Jewish Chronicle, said he preferred an Emirati Palestinian over a progressive Jew from Costa Rica, Rebeca Grynspan - as if the choice of secretary general boiled down to ethnicity.
True, everything that happens in Israel is ruled by ethnicity. Even Zionist Arabs are discarded as potential partners for government by the
opposition leaders
desperate to get rid of Netanyahu.
But happily, racism outside the pariah state has not yet descended to those depths.
Not a shoo-in
Unusually, with the backers she has secured, Nusseibeh is not a shoo-in for the top UN job.
There have now been
nine “straw polls”
, or informal soundings of the permanent and elected members of the Security Council, to determine who should replace Antonio Guterres as secretary general. Although these votes are cast anonymously, the
UK
,
France
and
China
, all permanent members, are believed to have
voted against Nusseibeh
.
In the latest poll on Friday, Nusseibeh received seven “encourage” votes, six “discourage” votes, and two “no opinion” votes - the same result she achieved on 6 November.
The process is opaque, and until now, no permanent member has formally cast a veto. But the selection of a successor appears deadlocked.
China is an advocate of the
principle of rotation
, and therefore favours a candidate from Latin America, but the reluctance of the UK and France to sign on the dotted line was unexpected.
No one needs a UN report to tell them what is happening in Sudan or Yemen.
The military defeats of western alliances in the last six interventions in the Middle East and Central Asia, should not lead anyone to rashly assume that the ideology of intervention has been abandoned. It’s simply easier all around to sell the franchise to Israel and the UAE.
At the same time, Abu Dhabi has been hard at work selling the myth that it represents the “model Arab” state of the future: a lip gloss of social liberalism covering a hard-baked, technologically cutting-edge dictatorship.
Not even
Iran
’s missiles and drones have punctured the myth that it’s “business as usual” again in Dubai and Abu Dhabi. The financial incentives for Britain to look the other way are enormous, when all that
blood gold
, and those blood diamonds from Africa, are laundered on their way to Moscow.
Lobbying pressure
Britain is locked in a tight embrace with the UAE. Some
250,000 expat Britons
work in Dubai and Abu Dhabi. More than
5,000 British companies
work in the Emirates as a whole. The UAE holds nearly £30bn ($39bn) of investment pledges in
more than 50 deals
.
Apart from
Manchester City
, it owns
P&O Ferries
, and holds an
eight percent stake
in Gatwick Airport. It also has stakes in the broadband provider CityFibre, parts of Berkeley Square in central London, and a major regeneration project in Manchester.
In the twilight years of neoliberalism, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham finds that his country has already flogged the Emiratis anything that was not nailed down, and much that was.
The biggest brake on Burnham changing anything radically in the relationship between Britain and its colonial creation is being applied by the Treasury, not the Foreign Office - although there are many there who are still in love with the UAE model.
Nusseibeh's first task would be to kill off the only international mechanism the world has left to calm things down, reintroduce stability and resolve conflicts
The UK’s presumed veto in the straw polls has put ferocious lobbying pressure on Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband.
The lobbying campaign for Nusseibeh has been relentless and wide-ranging. She came to visit former Conservative Party leader Iain Duncan Smith at his
office in Westminster
after he spoke out in parliament against the UAE’s involvement in Sudan and her candidacy.
Duncan Smith
denounced
the UAE’s “sponsoring of a huge amount of terrorism in Sudan”, and called on Britain to use its Security Council veto to block her nomination.
Interestingly, Nusseibeh reportedly
did not deny
to Duncan Smith that her country was funding and bankrolling the RSF.
Nusseibeh’s supporters in the UK wax lyrical about the qualities and energy of the 48-year-old diplomat.
“She’s charming. She’s extremely eloquent. She’s a fast thinker. She’s the best diplomat I’ve ever met,” one former British diplomat
told Middle East Eye
. “She’s assertive, and so she’s been good at articulating the UAE’s foreign policy position, which is that it has a right to be assertive.”
And, of course, she was educated at
Wycombe Abbey and Cambridge
- so that’s all right, then.
One source who
spoke to the Financial Times
said the choice was between principle and pragmatism. But that is exactly where the UK is going wrong.
Global recovery
Miliband and Burnham should be preparing the UK for the post-Trump era.
Today, it is funny to be a racist bigot in Israel. Elon Musk thinks it's a good look to throw the
weight of his satellites
around politics in the US and Ukraine, and into space, like some 16th-century buccaneer on a mission to discover the New World.
But in a very short time, today’s testosterone-fuelled, ego-driven strongman act is going to look so dated, and so ill-suited to the state the world is actually in. The neoliberal legacy, honed to extremes by Trump and his oligarchs, will be a weaker global economy, no real international order, and a chaos buffeted regularly by war, climate shocks and economic crashes.
The world will need a long period in which to recover, if indeed it ever does. It will have to rediscover the need for strong international institutions to feed populations, keep the peace, and rebuild postwar landscapes across the Middle East, Ukraine and Africa.
Why Britain must oppose UN candidacy of UAE's Nusseibeh
Read More »
It will need international rules and courts to adjudicate those rules, not nations that tear those rules up. The International Criminal Court and International Court of Justice will need to work around the clock.
The world will not need international courts cut down to size to protect war criminals in the US or Israel.
Putting Nusseibeh in place as secretary general would be to put her paymasters - the UAE and Israel - in charge of the UN.
These are the very pariah states that are actively working to spread conflict around the Middle East and Africa, and to subvert the institutions of the UN and
international law
for their own gain.
Israel is
starving Gaza
by keeping UN agencies at the Egyptian border, and
bombing aid workers
inside the territory. Can anyone imagine what Israel would do to the UN, and to all those fact-finding reports and investigations bubbling away inside, with its own candidate running the institution?
Nusseibeh’s first task would be to kill off the only international mechanism the world has left to calm things down, reintroduce stability and resolve conflicts.
It is pragmatism, not just principle, to oppose such a takeover. Britain, as a veto-wielding member of the Security Council, must hold firm.

items.title: Senior member of Turkish ruling party resigns amid fund probe
items.content:
ANKARA, Nov 24 (Reuters) - Hayati Yazici, a senior member and founder of Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan's ruling AK Party, said on Tuesday he was resigning from the party's leadership as a probe into alleged market manipulation and insider trading widened to include his son.
Since September, Turkish investment funds that had concentrated their holdings in thinly traded stocks have been unable to meet investor withdrawals, prompting regulators to liquidate 131 funds and launch a criminal probe that has involved several senior officials and members of government.

items.title: Life expectancy in Cuba falls for first time since 1950 amid economic crisis
items.content:
WHO chief says life expectancy has fallen from 78.8 years in 2020 to 74.4 in 2025, figures that predate US fuel blockade
Life expectancy has fallen for the first time in Cuba since 1950 as the island reels from a severe economic crisis, the head of the World Health Organization (WHO) said on Tuesday.
On a visit to Havana, the WHO chief, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said life expectancy had fallen from 78.8 years in 2020 to 74.4 years in 2025, the first decline since records began in 1950.

items.title: US judge permanently bars Trump from punishing rights groups who liaise with ICC
items.content:
US judge permanently bars Trump from punishing rights groups who liaise with ICC
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Tue, 11/24/2026 - 16:42
The president's executive order had put several US-based organisations at risk of fines and prison time
The International Criminal Court in The Hague (Remko De Waal/ANP/AFP)
Off
A US federal judge on Monday
permanently barred
the Trump administration from punishing rights groups who liaise with the International Criminal Court (ICC).
The ruling extends to all Americans, and not just the plaintiffs in the case.
Judge Jesse Furman of the Southern District of New York first issued a
temporary injunction
last month.
This week he ruled that while "the Government effectively requests that the Court reconsider its earlier decisions ... there is no merit to that request".
"Put simply, Plaintiffs demonstrate that the Services Prohibition is a content-based restriction on speech and that it is not narrowly tailored to serve compelling state interests," Furman wrote.
Democracy for the Arab World Now (Dawn), founded by the late Middle East Eye columnist Jamal Khashoggi, filed the lawsuit in July.
In October, Furman
blocked
the Trump administration from potentially imposing civil or criminal liability on the group as well as another allied organisation, the Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide (Taag), for any work carried out with the ICC.
"Anyone violating this prohibition could face up to 20 years in prison and up to $1 million in civil fines," Dawn said in a press release on Tuesday.
"Because the government can interpret the term 'services' to encompass anything that confers a benefit on the recipient, Americans before this ruling risked criminal prosecution for submitting evidence about possible crimes to the ICC, or for exchanging information with and engaging in joint advocacy with the Palestinian human rights groups and Special Rapporteur [Francesca] Albanese."
US judge bars Trump from punishing rights groups for liaising with ICC
Read More »
Albanese, the United Nations special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territories, has been sanctioned by the Trump administration since 2025.
"The permanent injunction strips the Trump administration of one of its most expansive tools - the power to jail or impose crippling fines on Americans for assisting the ICC and for working with groups who were sanctioned for demanding accountability for US and Israeli atrocity crimes - just weeks after the administration sanctioned the entire ICC," Dawn said.
"The court has affirmed that every American has the constitutional right to advocate for justice on Palestine without fear of reprisal."
Both Dawn and Taag confirmed they "will immediately move forward with ... ICC work and resume working closely with Special Rapporteur Albanese and the sanctioned Palestinian civil society groups".
Two weeks ago, Taag held a
press conference
at The Hague calling on the ICC to investigate Trump and his top diplomat Marco Rubio for "aiding and abetting genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity committed by Israel in Gaza".
US versus the ICC
In the early weeks of his presidency some 18 months ago, President Donald Trump signed
Executive Order 14203
, granting US officials the power to impose sanctions on foreigners for supporting the ICC's investigations into US and Israeli nationals for war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide.
He made it a federal offence to provide a "service" to, or receive one from, a sanctioned individual or entity.
ICC investigations, the Trump administration said, constitute a "national emergency" because the ICC lacks jurisdiction over crimes committed by US and Israeli nationals during wartime.
While Washington played a role in the early development of the ICC and signed the
Rome Statute
in 2000 under the presidency of Bill Clinton, it never submitted the statute to the Senate for ratification, amid fears that the ICC could prosecute US military personnel and officials for alleged war crimes, especially in conflicts in Afghanistan and Iraq.
Trump himself has been blunt about needing to punish the ICC for specifically
going after Israel
.
Using Executive Order 14203, Trump has so far sanctioned ICC
prosecutors and judges
, as well as the Palestinian
human rights groups
al-Haq, al-Mezan and the Palestinian Centre for Human Rights.

items.title: IRGC says it attacked container ship in Strait of Hormuz
items.content:
IRGC says it attacked container ship in Strait of Hormuz
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said its navy targeted a container ship in the Strait of Hormuz.
The IRGC said in a statement that it switched off its navigation and positioning systems, and the ship was “illegally” transiting through a restricted area north of Khasab in Oman.
“[We] once again emphasise to the owners and commanders of commercial vessels that adhering to maritime safety regulations, using authorised routes, and paying attention to warnings issued by relevant authorities are essential for ensuring the safety of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz,” the statement said.

items.title: Germany's left-wing Die Linke party expels pro-Palestine lawmaker
items.content:
Germany's left-wing Die Linke party expels pro-Palestine lawmaker
Germany's far-left Die Linke party on Tuesday expelled local pro-Palestine lawmaker Vanessa Emde over her criticism of Israel.
Die Linke, which came first in local elections in Berlin in September, has been trying to hammer out a coalition deal with the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD) and the Greens.
Emde was newly elected as a local representative from the Neukolln district, which has a large Arab population.
Emde's expulsion on Tuesday - which was backed by more than two-thirds of Die Linke's lawmakers in the Berlin parliament - clears one potential hurdle to sealing a coalition deal with the SPD and the Greens.
Member of Germany's far-left Die Linke party Vanessa Emde addresses protesters in Berlin on 31 October 2026 (AFP)

items.title: GCC condemns Houthi attack targeting Riyadh skyscraper
items.content:
GCC condemns Houthi attack targeting Riyadh skyscraper
Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi, secretary-general of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), has strongly condemned the “treacherous attack” launched by the Iran-aligned Houthis on a tower in Saudi capital Riyadh’s financial centre.
The attack injured 11 people - two Saudi citizens and nine foreign nationals.
“This attack is a heinous crime and an aggression that reveals the danger of this militia’s terrorist approach and its disregard for innocent lives, which requires a decisive international stance to hold this militia accountable,” Albudaiwi said in a statement.
He added that the GCC member states stand with Saudi Arabia.

items.title: Houthis won't seize Aden, Yemeni government forces say
items.content:
Houthis won't seize Aden, Yemeni government forces say
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis have pushed as close as 60km to Aden, the temporary capital of the country's internationally recognised government, but they will not capture the city, Yemen's military said on Tuesday.
"I'll speak to you frankly. The situation is not where we want it to be. But it's not as dire as reported," Colonel Majed Abdullah Al-Nuzaily, spokesperson for Yemen's armed forces, told a group of reporters via video link.
Since fighting resumed in Yemen in July in parallel with the wider Iran war, the Houthis have rapidly advanced in Yemen, seizing territory from the internationally recognised government and its allies, who are backed by Saudi Arabia.
The Saudis have carried out air strikes on Yemen in support of their allies on the ground, while the Houthis have struck Saudi oil targets, airports and office towers.
Aden, now the target of Houthi missile and drone strikes, had previously not seen major hostilities since street battles in 2015, soon after the internationally recognised government fled Houthi-run Sanaa and made the port city its base.
Reporting by Reuters

items.title: Eleven hurt in second Houthi strike within days on Riyadh's tallest tower
items.content:
Eleven hurt in second Houthi strike within days on Riyadh's tallest tower
Yemen's Houthis struck the tallest skyscraper in the Saudi capital Riyadh on Tuesday for the second time in less than a week, wounding at least 11 people.
Saudi Arabia's Civil Defence reported the injuries and posted a picture of the landmark tower housing the headquarters of the Saudi Public Investment Fund.
The image showed some damage to the building about halfway up the facade, similar to the impact from a strike on the same tower on 19 November, which caused damage but no injuries.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting against Yemen's Houthis said a skyscraper in Riyadh's financial district had been targeted by a "terrorist attack" without providing further details.

Iran adds 26 tugboats to Hormuz ‘non-compliance list’
Iran’s Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA) says it has added 26 tugboats to its “non-compliance list”, accusing them of providing services to offending vessels south of the Strait of Hormuz.
In a post on X, the PGSA listed tugboats registered in several countries, including the UAE, Singapore and India.
“As previously announced, vessels and companies that cooperate in providing services to offenders will themselves be placed on the non-compliance list,” it said.

items.content:
Exclusive: Records list 349 deaths in three years in Mali and also shed light on Russia’s military activity elsewhere in Africa
When the attack on Kidal began before dawn on 25 April this year, the Russian fighters were caught off guard. Within the first hour, checkpoints on the outskirts of the remote desert city nestled among the rocky hills of northern Mali had fallen to the insurgents, who pushed towards the police station where fierce fighting erupted.
“Everything was happening at once. Explosions were going off all around us, people were shouting,” recalled a former member of Russia’s Africa Corps who was stationed in Mali at the time and spoke on condition of anonymity. “Nobody knew where the enemy was coming from.”

items.title: Saudi finance minister claims kingdom can withstand prolonged Houthi conflict
items.content:
Saudi finance minister claims kingdom can withstand prolonged Houthi conflict
Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed al-Jadaan says the kingdom is “resilient enough to withstand a prolonged conflict” with Yemen’s Houthis.
Speaking to reporters, al-Jadaan dismissed as “a total mistake” any expectation that attacks on civilian infrastructure or “blackmail by missiles” would force Riyadh to compromise its national security.
He said Saudi Arabia plans to reduce its budget deficit to 3.6 percent of GDP in 2027, compared with an estimated 4.9 percent this year, despite the escalating fighting.
The Iran-backed Houthis say their missile and drone campaign aims to force Riyadh to withdraw support for Yemen’s government.
Al-Jadaan said reduced oil production had driven a 2.1 percent contraction in Saudi GDP this year.

items.title: 'Political theatre': Campaigners hit out at EU hypocrisy as Cop31 ends in chaos
items.content:
'Political theatre': Campaigners hit out at EU hypocrisy as Cop31 ends in chaos
Submitted by
Katherine Hearst
on
Tue, 11/24/2026 - 13:44
Developing countries say they felt kept in the dark and were not consulted during the drafting of the final text
Australian Minister for Climate Change and Energy and President of Cop31 Negotiations Chris Bowen at a plenary session at the UN Climate Change Conference in Antalya, Turkey, 22 November 2026 (Reuters)
Off
On Sunday, fraught global climate talks in
Turkey
, the longest ever in the climate conference’s history, ground to a halt, with
no deal
. The EU,
UK
and allies rejected the draft text over its failure to mention fossil fuels.
At the closing plenary, Ireland’s Climate Minister Darragh O’Brien, on behalf of the EU, rejected the text, saying it “does not respond to the science, and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required… that does not even mention fossil fuels”.
His words were met with applause. But they rang hollow for developing countries, many of whom also rejected the text over its weak language on climate finance.
After delivering his intervention, O’Brien and EU Climate Minister Wopke Hoekstra
walked out of the plenary to hold a press huddle
while developing nations were speaking about the need for climate finance.
While the EU, UK and allies cited the omission of fossil fuels from the text as their main reason for rejecting it, climate justice campaigners
reported
that developed countries and EU officials had spent the duration of the talks blocking measures which would require them to make fresh finance commitments.
“The EU used fossil fuels as the main reason for their rejection of the text. But the other issue, or what I would call the most important issue, is climate finance,” Harjeet Singh, strategic adviser to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative and the global convenor of the Fill the Fund campaign, told Middle East Eye.
“If you listened to what other countries said, like Panama, Ghana, the Marshall Islands, their reasons were no money for adaptation, no money for loss and damage.”
Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, developed countries are
required
to provide finance to help developing countries cut emissions and adapt to climate impacts.
According to the UN’s
latest report
, published earlier this month, developing countries will need about $300bn annually in adaptation funding by 2035.
At Cop26 in 2021, developed countries agreed to at least double adaptation finance by 2025, with 2019 levels, $19bn, as a benchmark.
Last year, they agreed to a call to “at least triple” adaptation finance by 2035. But the final text left ambiguities around the baseline year.
An earlier draft of this year’s text, released on 16 November, stipulated a target annual figure of at least $120bn, with a baseline of $40bn a year.
But the sums were quietly dropped from subsequent drafts. Climate justice campaigners laid the blame for this squarely at the doors of the EU and wealthier countries who they
say
"came with nothing" and thwarted progress on discussions around climate finance.
During this year’s “Contributor Dialogue” at the conference, which aimed to fill the starved fund, a handful of developed countries pledged just $30m, significantly down from last year’s sum of $120m.
“So we have a fund that no one wants to fill,” Singh said.
Dead in the water
Even before the summit had started, Hoekstra set the tone for negotiations by proclaiming climate finance “dead in the water”.
“They entered negotiations with that bad faith and blocked every single track which is important for developing countries,” Singh told MEE.
According to
Climate Action Network,
the EU and other developed countries refused to engage on a baseline for tripling adaptation finance.
Cop31 draft agreement ‘the worst ever', campaigners warn
Read More »
“We agreed on the baseline, I was witness to that process in 2019,” Singh said.
“So they just want to create new processes and new loops so that we can just continue talking.”
Singh also pointed to what he described as the hypocrisy of the EU and wealthy countries’ stance on fossil fuel language in the draft text.
"Norway and Ireland, who were arguing for the inclusion of fossil fuel language in the text, are back home expanding fossil fuel production,” he said.
The EU’s own “roadmaps” for transitions away from fossil fuels have drawn criticism for
restating existing policies
that are not aligned with the 1.5 degree temperature goal.
Brandon Wu, director of policy and campaigns at Action Aid USA,
slammed
the EU’s transition plans as a “smokescreen”.
“They’re using the rhetoric around fossil fuels to make themselves look like champions," Wu told reporters.
For Singh, a Cop veteran who has attended the last 18 conferences, the EU’s actions are tantamount to little more than “political theatre”.
“Do your work. We need to move beyond these theatrics and take real action, rather than simply claiming leadership. Be a real leader. Provide the money. Take action at home in line with your fair share of the global effort,” he said.
‘Extremely disrespected’
Campaigners told Middle East Eye that the talks’ meltdown was also due in part to the weak and untransparent facilitation by the joint presidents, Australia and Turkey.
“There was no stocktaking plenary where countries could share their opinion, where things could be dragged out in the open. When they said they would publish text, they didn’t do so,” Andreas Sieber, associate director of global policy at 350.org, told MEE.
'Norway and Ireland, who were arguing for the inclusion of fossil fuel language in the text, are back home expanding fossil fuel production'
- Harjeet Singh, strategic adviser to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative
MEE understands that many developing countries felt they were left in the dark and not consulted while the text was being drafted.
Cop presidents usually release printed versions of drafts for parties to review. But this year, only selected groups were shown excerpts, leaving many developing countries feeling “extremely disrespected and extremely badly treated,” one observer said.
Hanen Keskes of Greenpeace Mena said that the process of revising the second draft of the Cop text was very unclear.
“From what I've heard from parties, they had not been consulted,” Keskes told MEE. “It was very unclear what progress happened between the 19th and 22nd on other agenda items that were quite important.
“When the new text came out on Saturday night, it was essentially the same text from the 19th. So clearly no consultation had been done.”
The acrimony was summed up in a searing rebuke of the Cop presidency by Ghana’s Environment Minister Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings, who was “rudely cut off” during her delivery by Murat Kurum, Cop31 president and Turkey's environment minister.
“This excellency is an example of the levels of disrespect we have endured and continue to express our objection to. It absolutely does not respect multilateralism,” she said.
